assessment.name: Year 8 Maths Autumn assessment
assessment.sections: Tuesday 1 December: online (about 30 minutes). Wednesday 2 December: paper (45 minutes).
assessment.weighting: From the school Year 8 Maths Revision List: rounding, error intervals, estimation, percentages, fractions, decimals and percentages, expressions, indices, substitution, expanding, factorising and sequences. Equations and linear graphs are on the Spring list, so they are in the Spring deck. Sparx codes on each card lead to the videos.
assessment.equipment: Chromebook on Tuesday, pen, pencil, ruler, calculator

mock.note: 30 questions across the Autumn list. Work on paper as in the real test.

cards.title: Rounding to decimal places and significant figures
cards.question: How do you round to decimal places and to significant figures? (Sparx videos: M111, M431, M994, M131)
points: Decimal places: count digits after the decimal point. 3.476 to 1 dp = 3.5.
Significant figures: count from the first non-zero digit. 0.04821 to 2 sf = 0.048. 52 680 to 2 sf = 53 000.
Look at the next digit. 5 or more rounds up; 4 or less stays the same.
Keep place value with zeros when rounding large numbers.
cards.watch_out: Zeros at the start do not count as significant figures; zeros between digits do (4.07 has 3 sf).
cards.hook: 5 or more, raise the score. 4 or less, let it rest.
cards.grade9: Always check your rounded answer is about the same size as the original.

cards.title: Estimation
cards.question: How do you estimate the answer to a calculation? (Sparx videos: M878)
points: Round every number to 1 significant figure, then calculate.
Use ≈ to mean approximately equal to.
Say whether your estimate is an overestimate or underestimate by looking at how you rounded.
cards.watch_out: Do not use a calculator for estimation questions. Show the rounded numbers.
cards.hook: One sig fig, then work it out in your head.
cards.grade9: If you rounded one number up and one down in a division, explain the effect on the estimate.

cards.title: Error intervals
cards.question: How do you write the error interval of a rounded number? (Sparx videos: M730)
points: A length is 7.4 cm to 1 dp. The smallest it could be is 7.35; the largest is up to 7.45.
Error interval: 7.35 ≤ x < 7.45.
Halve the degree of accuracy, then subtract and add it.

example.heading: Worked example
lines: Mass = 60 kg to the nearest 10 kg

cards.watch_out: The lower bound is included, so use ≤ (less than or equal to). The upper bound is not included, because 7.45 rounds up to 7.5, so use < (less than).
cards.grade9: Combine bounds in a calculation by using the right bound for each part.

cards.title: Percentage of an amount
cards.question: How do you find a percentage of an amount with and without a calculator? (Sparx videos: M437, M905)
points: Without a calculator: 10% = ÷ 10, 1% = ÷ 100, 50% = ÷ 2, 25% = ÷ 4. Build up others.
With a calculator: multiply by the decimal. 17% of 250 = 0.17 × 250 = 42.5.
cards.watch_out: Percent means out of 100. 7% is 0.07, not 0.7.
cards.grade9: Choose the quickest method and show the build-up clearly for method marks.

cards.title: Percentage increase and decrease with multipliers
cards.question: How do you increase or decrease an amount by a percentage in one step? (Sparx videos: M476, M533)
points: Increase by 15%: multiply by 1.15. Decrease by 15%: multiply by 0.85.
cards.watch_out: For a decrease, the multiplier is 1 minus the decimal, not the decimal.
cards.hook: Up: 1 point something. Down: 0 point what's left.
cards.grade9: Use multipliers for repeated changes, for example 2 years of 5% growth = × 1.05².

cards.title: Percentage change and writing as a percentage
cards.question: How do you write one amount as a percentage of another, and find percentage change? (Sparx videos: M235)
points: As a percentage: part ÷ whole × 100. 18 out of 24 = 18 ÷ 24 × 100 = 75%.
Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100.
A price goes from £40 to £50: change £10, 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25% increase.
cards.watch_out: Always divide by the original amount, not the new amount.
cards.hook: Difference over Original, times one hundred (DOO).
cards.grade9: Explain in words what your percentage means in the context.

cards.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
cards.question: How do you convert between fractions, decimals and percentages? (Sparx videos: M958, M264, M553)
points: Percentage to decimal: divide by 100. 35% = 0.35. Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100. 0.6 = 60%.
Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom. 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.
Decimal to fraction: use place value, then simplify. 0.45 = 45/100 = 9/20.
Fraction to percentage: make the denominator 100, or convert to a decimal first. 7/20 = 35/100 = 35%.
cards.watch_out: 0.4 is 40%, not 4%. Each place to the right is ten times smaller, so check the place value.
cards.hook: Percent means per hundred: cent as in century.
cards.grade9: To order a mix of fractions, decimals and percentages, convert them all to decimals first.

cards.title: Simplifying expressions
cards.question: How do you simplify an algebraic expression? (Sparx videos: M795, M531, M120, M608)
points: Collect like terms: 3a + 5b − a + 2b = 2a + 7b.
Multiply: 3a × 4b = 12ab. a × a = a².
Index laws: a³ × a² = a⁵; a⁶ ÷ a² = a⁴.
Terms are separated by + and − signs. Keep the sign with the term after it.
cards.watch_out: a + a = 2a, but a × a = a².
cards.grade9: Check by substituting a number into both the original and your answer.

cards.title: Expanding and factorising
cards.question: How do you expand brackets and factorise expressions? (Sparx videos: M237, M792, M100)
points: Expand: multiply everything inside by the term outside. 3(2x − 5) = 6x − 15.
Expand and simplify: 2(x + 4) + 3(x − 1) = 2x + 8 + 3x − 3 = 5x + 5.
Factorise: take out the highest common factor. 12x + 18 = 6(2x + 3).
Factorise fully: 8a² − 12a = 4a(2a − 3).
cards.watch_out: A negative outside changes every sign inside. −2(x − 3) = −2x + 6.
cards.hook: Expand = open up. Factorise = put back in the box.
cards.grade9: Check factorising by expanding your answer back out.

cards.title: Substitution and formulae
cards.question: How do you substitute values into an expression or formula? (Sparx videos: M417, M327, M208)
points: Replace each letter with its number, using brackets for negatives.
Use BIDMAS: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.
cards.watch_out: Put negative numbers in brackets. (−2)² = 4, but −2² means −(2 × 2) = −4.
cards.hook: BIDMAS: Brackets, Indices, Divide, Multiply, Add, Subtract.
cards.grade9: Write each substitution step on a separate line.

cards.title: Term-to-term and special sequences
cards.question: What are term-to-term rules, and which special sequences should you know? (Sparx videos: M381, M241, M981)
points: Term-to-term rule: how to get from one term to the next. 5, 8, 11, 14: add 3.
Linear (arithmetic) sequences go up or down by the same amount.
Square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. Cube numbers 1, 8, 27, 64. Triangular numbers 1, 3, 6, 10, 15.
Fibonacci: add the two previous terms. 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13.
Geometric: multiply by the same number. 3, 6, 12, 24.
cards.watch_out: Check the difference between more than one pair of terms.
cards.grade9: Identify the type before trying to find a rule.

cards.title: The nth term of a linear sequence
cards.question: How do you find and use the nth term of a linear sequence? (Sparx videos: M991, M866)
points: The common difference goes in front of n.
Then find what to add or subtract to get the first term.
5, 8, 11, 14: difference 3, so 3n. When n = 1, 3n = 3, need +2. nth term = 3n + 2.
Use it: the 20th term = 3 × 20 + 2 = 62.
cards.watch_out: For decreasing sequences the difference is negative. 20, 17, 14 has nth term −3n + 23.
cards.hook: Difference times n, then fix the start (the zero term).
cards.grade9: Is 100 in the sequence 3n + 2? Solve 3n + 2 = 100. n = 32.67, not whole, so no.

cards.title: Using the nth term
cards.question: How do you generate terms from a formula and check if a number is in a sequence? (Sparx videos: M166)
points: Generate: substitute n = 1, 2, 3. For 4n − 1: 3, 7, 11, 15.
Check membership: set the nth term equal to the number and solve.
If n is a whole positive number, the number is in the sequence.

example.heading: Is 45 in 4n − 1?
lines: Not a whole number, so 45 is not in the sequence

cards.watch_out: Position (n) must be a whole number.
cards.grade9: Explain your reasoning in a full sentence.

cards.title: Methods to remember
cards.question: Can you recall each key method quickly?
points: Rounding: look at the next digit; 5 or more rounds up.
Percentage change = change ÷ original × 100. Multiplier up = 1 + %, down = 1 − %.
nth term: difference × n, then adjust.
Fraction to decimal: divide the top by the bottom. Decimal to percentage: × 100.
Special sequences: square 1, 4, 9; cube 1, 8, 27; triangular 1, 3, 6; Fibonacci 1, 1, 2, 3, 5.
cards.watch_out: Show working every time; method marks are given even if the final answer is wrong.
cards.grade9: Check answers with an estimate or by substituting back.

written.q: A coat costs £120. In a sale it is reduced by 30%. After the sale, the new price is increased by 30%. Is it back to £120? Show working.
model: No, because the 30% increase is of a smaller amount (1)

written.q: The nth term of a sequence is 7n − 4. Is 150 in the sequence? Explain.
model: Yes, because 22 is a whole number (1)

written.q: Estimate the value of 61.8 × 4.9 ÷ 0.52. Show your rounding.

exam_tips.timing: Online test about 30 minutes, paper test 45 minutes. Spend about 1 minute per mark.
section_a: Write down your working even in the online test, on scrap paper.
Estimate first so you know roughly what the answer should be.
Read the question again before you give the final answer, such as a length, not x.
section_b: Show every step; most marks are for method.
Use a ruler for graphs and label the axes.
Check by substituting answers back in.
grade9: Estimate before you calculate, then check the answer is sensible. 19% of 51 is about 10.
Change a percentage into the form that makes the sum easy: 15% = 0.15 = 15/100.
For a sequence find the change, then test a position rule. 4, 7, 10 gives 3n + 1.

mcq.e: The next digit is 7, so round up.
Count from the first non-zero digit.
